parts.title: Joining a fitness club
parts.context: A student phones a fitness club to ask about membership.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 1. You will hear a student phoning a fitness club to ask about membership. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: You will see that there is an example that has been done for you. On this occasion only, the conversation relating to this will be played first.

script.speaker: kelly
script.text: Riverside Fitness Club, Kelly speaking.

script.speaker: omar
script.text: Hello. I'd like some information about joining, please. I've been a bit lazy lately, and I want to get fitter.

script.speaker: kelly
script.text: Well, you've come to the right place. I'll take a few details first, and then I'll explain our memberships.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: The caller wants to get fitter, so 'fitter' has been written in the space. Now we shall begin. You should answer the questions as you listen, because you will not hear the recording a second time. Listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: kelly
script.text: Could I have your name, please?

script.speaker: omar
script.text: It's Omar Haddad. That's H-A-D-D-A-D.

script.speaker: kelly
script.text: Thank you, Omar. And what do you do? Are you working?

script.speaker: omar
script.text: No, I'm a student at the university. I'm in my second year.

script.speaker: kelly
script.text: That's useful to know, because we have a special rate for students. Is there anything in particular you'd like to try?

script.speaker: omar
script.text: I used to do boxing, but I'd rather try something new. My sister recommended your yoga classes, so I'd like to start with those.

script.speaker: kelly
script.text: They're very popular. And when would you be most likely to come?

script.speaker: omar
script.text: Mostly in the mornings, before my lectures start. The evenings are difficult because of my part-time job.

script.speaker: kelly
script.text: That's fine; the club opens at six. Have you been a member of a gym before?

script.speaker: omar
script.text: Yes, in Leeds, before I moved here, but that was two years ago.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: kelly
script.text: Right, I'll tell you about our memberships. Basic membership is twenty-five pounds a month, and that's for the gym only. Standard membership is thirty-five pounds, and as well as the gym, it includes any of our classes.

script.speaker: omar
script.text: And the student rate?

script.speaker: kelly
script.text: That's thirty pounds a month, and it includes the gym, the classes and the swimming pool, so for you it's the best value. You'll need to show your student card when you join.

script.speaker: omar
script.text: That sounds good. Is there a joining fee?

script.speaker: kelly
script.text: Yes. It's normally fifty pounds, but we're reducing it to forty pounds this month. You pay it once, when you join, and it doesn't come back.

script.speaker: omar
script.text: Can I try the club before I decide?

script.speaker: kelly
script.text: Of course. We can give you a free day pass. Just bring some identification, and come at any time that suits you. Shall I book you in for tomorrow morning?

script.speaker: omar
script.text: Yes, please. Thank you for your help.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 1. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: A science festival
parts.context: An organiser tells visitors where events take place and how the festival works.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 2. You will hear an organiser telling visitors about a science festival. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: hartley
script.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the Riverside Science Festival. I'm Jean Hartley, one of the organisers. Let me tell you what's happening, and where.

script.speaker: hartley
script.text: Our most popular event is the robot football tournament, which takes place in the Main Hall. Teams from six schools have built their own robots, and the final is at three o'clock.

script.speaker: hartley
script.text: If you'd like to learn about the stars, there's a space show in the Planetarium, which is the round building behind the car park. It's a twenty-minute film, shown every hour.

script.speaker: hartley
script.text: For those who prefer to get their hands dirty, the chemistry workshop will be held in Lab One. Please wear the safety glasses that are provided, and no running in the lab.

script.speaker: hartley
script.text: The dinosaur talk is in the Atrium, which is the glass-roofed area at the entrance. A real palaeontologist will bring some fossils, and you may touch them, if you're careful.

script.speaker: hartley
script.text: And for the younger visitors, there's a coding game in Room Twelve, on the first floor. No experience is needed. The Garden, by the way, is where the picnic area is, but there are no events there, and the Library is closed for the whole festival.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: hartley
script.text: Now, some practical information. Entry to the festival is free, and so are all the workshops. Please don't pay anybody at the gate, because there's no charge, although donations are welcome.

script.speaker: hartley
script.text: The one exception is the space show. Because the Planetarium only has eighty seats, you need to book a ticket in advance at the information desk, and tickets go quickly, so I'd suggest doing that straight away.

script.speaker: hartley
script.text: We're open from ten until five every day, except on Saturday, when the festival stays open until nine, with a special science night. There'll be live music and a talk by an astronaut.

script.speaker: hartley
script.text: If you've brought large bags or a pushchair, you can leave them in the cloakroom, next to the information desk. The cloakroom is free, and it's staffed all day.

script.speaker: hartley
script.text: Finally, there's a quiz trail around the festival. Pick up a form at the entrance and answer ten questions. Everyone who completes it receives a badge, and the best forms win a book. Have a wonderful day.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 2. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: A dissertation on urban green spaces
parts.context: A student discusses her dissertation with her supervisor.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 3. You will hear a student, Isla, discussing her dissertation on urban green spaces with her supervisor, Dr Mensah. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: mensah
script.text: Isla, thanks for coming in. I've read the draft of your first chapters, and overall it's coming along well. Tell me how the survey went.

script.speaker: isla
script.text: I wanted two hundred responses, and I got two hundred and twelve in the end. The problem was getting people to finish. Most of the paper forms came back half-empty, so I switched to an online version, and that worked much better.

script.speaker: mensah
script.text: Good. And the sample? Are the residents representative?

script.speaker: isla
script.text: Mostly older people answered. Only about ten percent were under thirty, which isn't ideal.

script.speaker: mensah
script.text: Then say so clearly in the limitations section. Don't hide it. A weakness that you explain is much better than one that I have to find.

script.speaker: isla
script.text: OK. Another problem is the literature review. There's a huge amount published on parks and health, and I don't know how much to include.

script.speaker: mensah
script.text: Focus on studies from cities similar to yours, in the last ten years. Don't try to cover everything.

script.speaker: isla
script.text: I've found one study that says the opposite of my results. Should I leave it out?

script.speaker: mensah
script.text: Certainly not. Explain why your results are different. That's the kind of discussion that earns marks.

script.speaker: isla
script.text: And the deadline is the fifteenth of April, isn't it?

script.speaker: mensah
script.text: That's right, but I'd like to see a full draft by the end of March, so I can give you proper feedback.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: mensah
script.text: Let's go through your structure, so I know what to expect. What's in the first chapter?

script.speaker: isla
script.text: A summary of the existing literature on green spaces and health, as you suggested.

script.speaker: mensah
script.text: And the second?

script.speaker: isla
script.text: That's the survey: how I designed it, who answered, and what they said.

script.speaker: mensah
script.text: Then?

script.speaker: isla
script.text: Chapter three has maps of the five parks I visited. I've marked where people sit, walk and meet, using different colours.

script.speaker: mensah
script.text: That could be striking. And chapter four?

script.speaker: isla
script.text: Interviews. I talked to the park managers, to find out why people use some parks more than others.

script.speaker: mensah
script.text: Good, that will help to explain your results. And the end?

script.speaker: isla
script.text: A short conclusion, with three recommendations for the council. I've cut my photographs, to keep the word count down.

script.speaker: mensah
script.text: Sensible. Send me chapter one by Friday.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 3. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Lecture: how animals sleep
parts.context: A biology lecture on sleep in animals, from bats to dolphins.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 4. You will hear a lecture about how animals sleep. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Good afternoon. Sleep is one of the great puzzles of biology. Every animal that has been carefully studied seems to sleep in some way, yet they do it in remarkably different ways.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Take the amount of sleep. Bats are the champions: some species sleep for up to twenty hours a day, hanging upside down in caves. At the other extreme, giraffes need only a few hours, and they often take short naps while standing up.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Then there's the problem of safety, because a sleeping animal is vulnerable. Dolphins have found a solution. They sleep with only half of the brain at a time, while the other half stays awake. That way a dolphin can keep swimming and come to the surface to breathe, and the two halves take turns.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Some birds do something similar. Frigatebirds spend weeks at sea without landing, and researchers have recorded them sleeping while flying, in naps that last a few seconds. Altogether, they sleep for less than an hour a day, much less than on land.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: A more recent discovery concerns fur seals. In the water they sleep with half of the brain, like dolphins, but when they come on to land, they sleep with both halves, just as we do.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: So why do animals sleep at all? There are two main theories. One says that sleep gives the brain a chance to clear away waste products that build up during the day. The other says that sleep helps the brain to store memories, by going over the day's experiences. There is evidence for both.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: What we do know is that sleep is essential. In a famous experiment, rats that were kept awake died within about three weeks, which is sooner than they would have died of hunger. But research continues, because many questions remain unanswered. For next week, please read the chapter on dreaming.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 4. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of the Listening test.
